title: Dry skin and the skin barrier
summary: Dry skin feels tight, rough or flaky because it is losing water faster than usual. Simple habits help most: short lukewarm showers, a gentle cleanser used only where needed, and moisturiser applied soon after washing and several times a day.

what_it_is: The outer layer of the skin works as a barrier that holds water in and keeps irritants out. Hot water, harsh soaps, dry air and some products weaken it, and then the skin feels tight and flaky.
Dryness can also go with eczema, psoriasis and other conditions, and occasionally it is a sign of an underlying health condition.
may_contribute: Long or hot showers and baths.
Dry air from heaters or air conditioning, and cold weather.
Products with alcohol or fragrance, and some strong active ingredients.
Age, and the skin condition eczema.
self_care: Keep showers and baths to about five to ten minutes in warm, not hot, water, and pat the skin dry, leaving it slightly damp.
Use a mild, fragrance-free cleanser, and only where needed. A leave-on moisturiser can replace soap for washing.
Moisturise soon after washing and several times a day. Creams and ointments usually hold in water better than lotions; very dry skin often does best with an ointment.
Choose products labelled fragrance-free. Unscented products can still contain ingredients that mask smell.
A humidifier in the bedroom can help in dry air; clean it regularly.
Wear gloves for wet tasks and in cold weather, and choose loose cotton clothing.
Use sunscreen on exposed skin every day.
avoid: Alcohol-based and fragranced products on dry skin.
Aqueous cream as a moisturiser or soap substitute, because it can irritate the skin.
monitor: Note how often moisturiser is applied and whether the skin feels better within about two weeks.
see_clinician: The dryness continues after trying these steps for a couple of weeks.
The skin is painful, cracked, bleeding, stinging or very itchy.
Patches are red, thick or scaly, which can be eczema or psoriasis.
A product causes burning, stinging or irritation.
urgent: Oozing, crusting, pus, increasing redness or warmth, or a fever can mean an infection and need prompt assessment.
photo_limits: A photo cannot tell ordinary dryness from eczema, psoriasis or a fungal infection.

terms.plain: a moisturiser that soothes dry skin and holds water in
the outer layer of skin that holds water in and keeps irritants out

limitations: General education, not a diagnosis. Dryness that does not improve can point to another condition.
Moisturisers can catch fire easily on clothing and bedding: keep them away from flames and cigarettes, and take cream from a tub with a clean spoon.
claims_to_verify: Showers of about five to ten minutes in warm water are appropriate advice for the clinic's patients and climate.
Stating that ointments suit very dry skin better than lotions is appropriate, and the NHS advice that ointments should not be used on weeping eczema is respected elsewhere.
